title: Org-aware circuit breakers and quota model for tenant routing
content:
Purpose:

This doc captures a proposal for adding org-aware circuit breakers and a flexible quota model into the platform routing/control plane. Goal is to provide predictable SLAs for paying customers, automatic noisy-neighbor mitigation, and safe multi-region failover, while minimizing false positives that harm healthy tenants. This is an operational-first, incremental design aimed at landing in the next two quarters.

Background / why now:
- We have recurring incidents where a small set of tenants induce wide performance regressions (bursting request patterns, heavy long-sequence generations).
- Current per-replica rate limiting is too coarse: it doesn’t respect contract tiers, regional residency, or cross-tenant fairness.
- Dedicated and Private customers expect strict isolation and SLAs; hosted customers expect predictable performance by tier.
- Need to reduce manual runbook interventions.

Design goals (non-exhaustive):
- SLA alignment: allow policies that guarantee soft/hard limits aligned to contract tiers (free / standard / enterprise).
- Graceful degradation: observability and rollback-first behaviours (circuit breakers that fail to cheaper model variant or queue rather than drop).
- Multi-region awareness: prefer region affinity but allow contract-aware failover (enterprise routes to secondary region earlier than free tier).
- Low operational overhead: simple telemetry to understand who caused ejection / throttling decisions.

High-level concepts:
- Tenant identity: runtime requests carry a tenant_id and contract_tier attribute (populated from control plane).
- Policy Engine: a centralized policy store (versioned) that control plane components consult to make routing/throttling decisions. Policies are feature-flagged for rollout.
- Soft quota vs hard quota: soft quota triggers backpressure signals (queue, slow-path, suggest model-quantization), hard quota enforces strict rejection or circuit-breaker open.
- Local fast-path: edge routing enforces quick checks (token bucket per-tenant, short window burst control). Control plane agent on-node does longer-window accounting and can eject at pool-level.
- Circuit breaker states: CLOSED (normal), SOFT_OPEN (apply degradations), HARD_OPEN (reject), COOL_DOWN (probe). State machine transitions are driven by both local metrics and control-plane decisions.

Quota model (proposal):
- Per-tenant baseline budget: tokens/minute (align to contract). Example: free=100k tokens/min, standard=1M, enterprise=5M.
- Burst bucket: short-term allowance to absorb spikes (token bucket with burst size = baseline * burst_factor). Default burst_factor = 2 for standard, 1.2 for enterprise (we assume enterprise gets predictable steady throughput).
- Banked credits: unused monthly budget may be banked up to 2x baseline for a limited window. This is important for tenants with periodic heavy jobs. Controlled by billing integration.
- Priority queue weight: when contention occurs, queue prioritization uses (contract_priority, recency_of_traffic, tenancy_health_score).
- Soft quota actions: throttled responses that include Retry-After header; automatic non-blocking fallback to lower-cost model variants or cached responses when configured.
- Hard quota actions: HTTP 429 with tenant-scoped reason; trigger alert to account owner and ops. For enterprise customers a configurable grace/override token route exists via support.

Noisy-neighbor mitigation patterns:
1) Local per-pool tenant ejection: if tenant consumes >X% of GPU cycles for Y minutes and causes median latency to exceed SLO, mark tenant as ejected from that pool and route to dedicated fallback (lower priority) or slow-path (queue).
2) Backpressure propagation: worker nodes emit local backpressure flags upstream (edge router), which can trigger immediate per-tenant throttles on ingress to avoid overload cascades.
3) Adaptive batching limits: dynamically reduce max-batch-size for tenants that increase latency variance.
4) Predictive throttling: using recent token burn trends combined with ML heuristic to preemptively apply soft limits before SLO breaches. (proto in R&D backlog)

Multi-region routing considerations:
- Region affinity: default to tenant's preferred region for data locality and legal.
- Contract-aware failover: tier-based failover policies — enterprise tenants failover to secondary region after shorter detection windows; free tenants have longer windows or are rate-limited to best-effort.
- Graceful cold-start: when failing over to a region without warm cache/KV, apply a slower ramp and prefer cached model variants or shorter sequences.
- Cross-region quotas: maintain a global logical budget but enforce region-local quotas to avoid bursting one region. Control plane reconciles with eventual consistency semantics and exposes recent replication lag.

Control plane and runtime integration:
- Policy store: git-backed policy repository (YAML) + admin UI. Policies include tier mappings, quotas, ejection thresholds, and failover preferences.
- Versioned rollout: policy versions are staged (canary -> region rollout -> global). Rollouts are tied to a policy-change PR with automated smoke tests.
- Local agent: each routing node runs a lightweight agent that caches policies and reports usage; it enforces fast-path checks and forwards long-window accounting to the control plane.
- Telemetry: per-tenant time-series (qps, token burn, p50/p95 latency per model), ejection events, and circuit-breaker state transitions. Store in metrics DB with tenant tag.

Operational signals and alerts:
- Pager thresholds: when >5% of production tenants are in SOFT_OPEN in a region => P1.
- Tenant-specific: when an enterprise tenant enters HARD_OPEN => P0 + auto-notify account SA and CS.
- Drift alerts: if actual token burn > billed tokens for a tenant (billing integration mismatch) -> ops alert + blocked post-pay overspend guard.

SLO mapping and billing interaction:
- Map quotas to SLO tiers. E.g., standard tier gets p95 latency target under baseline budget; exceeding budget moves routing into degradations but does not immediately violate SLA unless it hits HARD_OPEN and causes consistent errors.
- Billing tie-in: banked credits, burst overages tracked and emitted in usage records; ops can issue temporary overrides for enterprise customers.

Example policy snippet (YAML-like pseudo-config, plain text):

policy_version: v3
tenants:
  - tenant_id: acme-corp
    contract_tier: enterprise
    baseline_tokens_per_min: 5000000
    burst_factor: 1.25
    bankable: true
    preferred_region: us-west-2
    failover_policy: immediate-to-secondary
    ejection_thresholds:
      pool_cpu_pct: 65
      duration_mins: 3
      latency_p95_ms: 600

  - tenant_id: hobbyapp
    contract_tier: free
    baseline_tokens_per_min: 100000
    burst_factor: 2.0
    bankable: false
    preferred_region: us-east-1
    failover_policy: best-effort

Rolling this policy: PR -> canary (5% of users on us-west) for 24h -> check metrics table (tenant_ejections, p95) -> region rollout if stable.

Runbook sketch (when a pool shows latency spike):
1) Check per-tenant leaderboard (who is burning tokens?).
2) If single tenant > 50% of cycles, mark as candidate for local ejection and open a soft ticket to customer.
3) If many tenants contributing, raise capacity/autoscale or enable global backpressure (temporary).
4) Use policy override to reduce burst_factor for problematic tenants for 1h.

Rollout plan / milestones:
- Phase 0 (2 weeks): implement metric collection + per-tenant token counters (no enforcement).
- Phase 1 (4 weeks): local fast-path hard/soft token buckets (edge), with admin kill-switch for safety.
- Phase 2 (8 weeks): control-plane policy store + ejection signals and telemetry integration.
- Phase 3 (ongoing): contract-aware multi-region failover and banked-credit integration with billing.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Accuracy vs latency of control-plane decisions: eventually-consistent control plane simplifies scaling but can misclassify during replication lag. Mitigation: local defaults + last-writer-wins policy timestamps.
- Complexity of banked credits: adds accounting complexity and potential billing disputes. Need clear UI and audit logs.
- How aggressively to prefer model-degradation vs reject? Default should be degrade -> queue -> reject. But some enterprise SLAs may require reject-first if predictability is more valuable.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add end-to-end test harness that simulates tenant bursts and measures ejection false positive rate. (JIRA: PLAT-842)
- Sync with billing on banked-credit semantics and UI display.
- Draft customer-facing doc for enterprise account managers explaining failover and override process.
- Prototype ML-based predictive throttle in applied-ml backlog.

References / related docs:
- tenant-routing-controls-architectural-sketch (prior sketch)
- org-capacity-buckets-and-backpressure-routing (capacity ideas overlap)
- CONFLUENCE link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Tenant+Routing+Home

Quick notes (choppy, for later):
- prefer soft-open hooks to call lower-cost model variant first (save cost + maintain latency)
- make ejection events human-readable in console (who/why/when)
- admin override should be auditable (who pressed the button)

End of doc.
